43617: In a world without electric light, a lamp meant safety, life and the ability to see the way. The seven-branched golden lampstand in the tabernacle stood for God's light among his people, and later the churches are pictured as lampstands giving light to the world.
43618: God's light and presence in the sanctuary
43619: The lampstand burned continually before the LORD; its almond-blossom design may echo a flowering tree.
43621: Scripture is a lamp for one's feet: enough light for the next step.
43623: God promises David 'a lamp' in Jerusalem, meaning his dynasty will not be snuffed out.
43625: Zechariah's lampstand is fed by the Spirit; in Revelation the seven lampstands are explicitly the seven churches, and the two witnesses are two lampstands.
43627: Keeping lamps burning means being ready for the Master's return.
43628: The menorah in the tabernacle and Solomon's ten lampstands (1 Kgs 7:49) mark God's dwelling. The lamp is also a picture of human life ('the lamp of the wicked will be put out', Prov 24:20) and of David's dynasty.
43629: Jesus warns not to hide a lamp under a basket (Mark 4:21), calls John the Baptist 'a burning and shining lamp' (John 5:35), and threatens to remove the Ephesian church's lampstand if it does not repent (Rev 2:5). In the new Jerusalem the Lamb is its lamp (Rev 21:23).
43630: The Hanukkah lampstand (nine branches) is a later Jewish development; the biblical menorah has seven lamps.
43634: Whoever holds the keys controls who gets in and who stays out. In the Bible keys picture authority: to open and shut the king's house, the kingdom of heaven, or even death itself.
43635: Delegated authority in the king's house
43636: Eliakim, the palace steward, receives the key of David's house; Revelation applies this key to the risen Christ.
43637: Keys of the kingdom given to Peter
43638: Catholics read this as a unique, continuing office passed to Peter's successors, the popes. Orthodox usually see Peter as first among equals and the keys shared by all bishops. Protestants commonly link the keys to preaching the gospel and church discipline exercised by the whole church (Matt 18:18 gives binding and loosing to the disciples generally).
43640: Jesus accuses the lawyers of taking away the key of knowledge: neither entering nor letting others in.
43642: Jesus holds the keys of death and Hades; an angel receives the key of the bottomless pit.
43643: Keys are rare in the Old Testament; the key passage is Isaiah 22, where palace authority passes from Shebna to Eliakim.
43644: Matthew 16 (Peter), Luke 11 (key of knowledge) and Revelation's keys of David, death and the abyss.
43645: Matthew 16:19 is a classic flashpoint between Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant views of church authority; read each position at its best. See /debates/scripture-and-tradition.
43647: A crown marks a king, a priest set apart, or a winner at the games. In the Bible it stands for royal rule, honour, and the reward God gives to the faithful; it also appears mocking Jesus as a crown of thorns.
43649: Christ returns wearing 'many diadems', the Greek word for royal crowns.
43651: The high priest's turban bore a gold plate called the 'holy crown'. Zechariah crowns the high priest Joshua in a sign of a coming priest-king.
43653: Humanity is crowned with glory; a good wife, grey hair and grandchildren are crowns.
43655: Paul uses the athlete's victory wreath. Whether these 'crowns' are distinct rewards or different ways of describing eternal life itself is debated.
43657: Soldiers crown Jesus with thorns; John's Gospel presents the mock coronation as ironically true.
43658: Crowns belong to kings and to the high priest, and are used figuratively for honour. Losing one's crown means disgrace (Lam 5:16).
43659: Mostly stephanos, the victor's wreath, for believers' reward, and the crown of thorns. The elders cast their crowns before God's throne (Rev 4:10), giving their honour back to him.
43660: The sword is the main weapon of ancient war, so it means violence, judgement and the power of rulers. The Bible also uses it for God's word, which cuts deep and judges truly.
43662: Sword, famine and plague are the standard triad of covenant curses.
43664: The Spirit's sword is the word of God; the returning Christ conquers with a sword from his mouth, not one in his hand.
43665: Authority of the state to punish
43666: The ruler 'does not bear the sword in vain'. How far this justifies war or capital punishment divides Christian traditions, especially pacifist and just-war ones.
43668: Jesus says he brings 'not peace but a sword', meaning his call will divide families. Simeon tells Mary a sword will pierce her soul.
43670: A flaming sword guards the way to the tree of life.
43671: Swords fill Israel's battle narratives. The prophets look forward to swords beaten into ploughshares (Isa 2:4; Mic 4:3), though Joel reverses the image for the final battle (Joel 3:10).
43672: Peter's sword in Gethsemane is rebuked: 'all who take the sword will perish by the sword' (Matt 26:52). The 'two swords' of Luke 22:38 are debated: literal self-defence, or a sign that the disciples misunderstood. Paul's armour image includes the sword of the Spirit.
43673: Medieval 'two swords' theory (spiritual and temporal power) built a whole political theology on Luke 22:38; most interpreters today think that goes far beyond the verse.
43677: A trumpet blast gathered people, warned of danger, started battles, crowned kings and announced holy days. In the Bible it signals that God is acting: at Sinai, at Jericho, and at the end of the age when the dead are raised.
43679: Silver trumpets assembled the camp; the watchman blows the trumpet to warn of attack.
43681: At Sinai a very loud trumpet sound grew louder as God descended.
43683: The ram's horn announced the year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and land returned.
43685: Jericho's walls fall at the trumpet; kings were proclaimed with it.
43686: The end of the age and resurrection
43687: The 'last trumpet' raises the dead. Revelation's seven trumpets announce escalating judgements.
43688: Ram's horn and silver trumpets mark worship, war, coronation and the Day of Trumpets. The prophets use the trumpet for the coming day of the LORD.
43689: Trumpets accompany Christ's return, the resurrection, and the seven judgements of Revelation 8 to 11.
43690: Whether Paul's 'last trumpet' is the same as Revelation's seventh trumpet, and how either fits a timeline of rapture and tribulation, is debated; see /debates/rapture.
43691: A seal was a carved stone or ring pressed into clay or wax. It proved who owned or authorised something and kept it closed. The Bible uses it for ownership, protection, authenticity and secrets kept until the right time.
43693: Letters and deeds were valid when sealed with the owner's seal.
43695: God's servants are marked on the forehead and spared from judgement.
43696: The Holy Spirit as God's seal
43697: The Spirit marks believers as God's and guarantees their future. Whether this sealing implies the believer can never fall away is part of the /debates/eternal-security discussion.
43699: Daniel is told to seal his book; in Revelation only the Lamb can open the sealed scroll, and John is told not to seal his.
43701: Circumcision was a seal of the righteousness Abraham had by faith. Some traditions apply this to baptism.
43702: Royal and personal seals appear in Genesis (Judah's signet, Gen 38:18), Kings, Esther and Jeremiah. Daniel's den was sealed (Dan 6:17); the beloved asks to be set 'as a seal upon your heart' (Song 8:6).
43703: Jesus' tomb is sealed (Matt 27:66); the Father has 'set his seal' on the Son (John 6:27); the Spirit seals believers; Revelation has seven seals opened by the Lamb.
43706: An animal's horn is its weapon and the sign of its strength. In the Bible a horn can be a literal container for oil, the corners of the altar, or a picture of power, especially royal power. In Daniel and Revelation horns are kings.
43708: To 'lift up the horn' is to be strengthened or vindicated; God is the 'horn of my salvation'.
43710: Zechariah praises God for raising 'a horn of salvation' in David's house.
43712: Daniel's angel explains that horns are kings. The Lamb with seven horns (Rev 5:6) has complete power.
43714: Samuel and Zadok anoint kings from a horn of oil.
43715: Horns of the altar: atonement and refuge
43716: Blood was put on the altar's horns; a fugitive grasping them sought mercy, though the law did not protect deliberate murderers (Exod 21:14).
43717: Horn imagery runs from Hannah's song and the Psalms (strength) to the altar's corner horns and the ram caught by its horns in place of Isaac (Gen 22:13).
43718: Only Luke 1:69 outside Revelation; in Revelation the Lamb, the dragon and the beasts all have horns, showing a contest of powers.
43719: Identifying the 'little horn' of Daniel 7 and 8 is debated: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (most critical and many conservative scholars for Dan 8), a future antichrist, or the papacy (a historic Protestant reading). See /debates/millennium.
43724: Ancient books were rolled scrolls of leather or papyrus. In the Bible a scroll stands for God's recorded word, his plan for history, and his record of people and their deeds, including the 'book of life'.
43726: God's register of those who belong to him. Whether names can be blotted out is part of the /debates/eternal-security discussion.
43728: Books are opened at the judgement; God remembers those who fear him.
43730: Only the Lamb is worthy to open the sealed scroll, so only Christ unlocks and carries out God's purposes.
43732: Prophets eat a scroll: sweet in the mouth but sometimes bitter in the stomach, because the message includes judgement.
43734: The sky is rolled up like a scroll at the end.
43735: Moses writes the law in a book (Exod 24:7; Deut 31:24-26); Josiah's reform starts when the book of the law is found (2 Kgs 22:8-13); King Jehoiakim cuts and burns Jeremiah's scroll, which is rewritten (Jer 36).
43736: Jesus reads from the Isaiah scroll in Nazareth (Luke 4:17-21). Revelation's sealed scroll, little scroll and books of judgement form a major thread. Paul asks Timothy for his scrolls and parchments (2 Tim 4:13).
43739: A shepherd's staff, a walking stick, a ruler's sceptre and a rod for correction were all similar wooden sticks. So the rod stands for authority, guidance and protection, and sometimes for discipline or punishment.
43740: God's power working through a leader
43741: Moses' ordinary shepherd's staff becomes 'the staff of God' through which signs are done.
43743: The sceptre will not depart from Judah; the Messiah rules the nations with a rod of iron.
43745: The rod drove off predators and the staff guided the sheep; both comfort.
43747: Aaron's staff buds, blossoms and bears almonds, settling who is the true priest; it was kept in the ark.
43749: Fathers and God himself discipline with the rod; Assyria is the rod of God's anger.
43750: Staffs of Moses and Aaron, the sceptre of Judah, the shepherd's rod and the rod of correction all appear. Isaiah's 'rod out of the stem of Jesse' (Isa 11:1, KJV) is a different word meaning a shoot.
43751: Jesus sends the disciples out with only a staff (Mark 6:8). Revelation applies Psalm 2's iron rod to Christ and his faithful people, and John measures the temple with a measuring rod (Rev 11:1).
43752: Whether the Proverbs 'rod' passages endorse physical punishment of children today is debated: some read them as permanent instruction, others as ancient wisdom about discipline in general that need not mean hitting.
43754: A yoke is the wooden beam that joins two oxen so they can pull a plough together. It became a picture of being under someone's control, whether a cruel master or a kind teacher, and of working in partnership.
43756: God broke Israel's yoke in Egypt; Jeremiah wore a yoke to act out submission to Babylon.
43757: Obligation to God and his law
43758: Jewish teachers spoke of taking on 'the yoke of the kingdom of heaven' (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). At the Jerusalem council Peter calls law-keeping as a requirement for Gentiles a yoke too heavy to bear.
43760: Jesus invites the weary to take his yoke: becoming his disciple brings rest, not a heavier load.
43761: Do not be 'unequally yoked'; Paul calls a coworker his 'true yokefellow'.
43762: Mostly a picture of foreign domination and of God's freeing his people. Isaiah 58:6 calls true fasting breaking every yoke.
43763: Jesus' gentle yoke, Paul's warning against a 'yoke of slavery', and the image of believers as yoked partners.
43764: 2 Corinthians 6:14 is often applied to marriage between a believer and unbeliever; the context is broader (partnership with idolatry), though many still apply it to marriage.
43766: An altar is a raised place where offerings were made to God. It marked meeting with God, remembering what he had done, and atonement for sin through sacrifice.
43768: The patriarchs built altars where God appeared to them.
43770: Blood on the altar made atonement because 'the life is in the blood'.
43772: An altar could be a witness rather than a place of sacrifice; altars were named 'The LORD is my banner' and 'The LORD is peace'.
43774: In Revelation the martyrs cry out under the altar and the prayers of the saints rise from it.
43776: Catholic and Orthodox Christians often connect this with the Eucharistic table; many Protestants read it as Christ and his cross, since Hebrews stresses that Christ's sacrifice was once for all. Debated.
43777: From Noah and Abraham to the bronze altar of the tabernacle and temple, altars structure Israel's worship. Unauthorised altars and pagan altars are condemned (1 Kgs 12:32-33; 2 Kgs 23:15).
43778: Jesus tells worshippers to reconcile before offering at the altar (Matt 5:23-24). Hebrews presents Christ's single sacrifice as replacing repeated offerings; Paul urges believers to offer themselves as 'living sacrifices' (Rom 12:1).
43782: Incense is fragrant resin burned to produce sweet smoke. In the tabernacle it was offered morning and evening before God, and the Bible links its rising smoke to prayer rising to God.
43783: The people prayed outside while Zechariah offered incense; in Revelation the golden bowls of incense are the prayers of the saints.
43785: The holy incense had a set recipe and was not for private use. Nadab and Abihu died offering 'strange fire'.
43787: On the Day of Atonement incense clouded the mercy seat; Aaron's censer stopped a plague as he stood between the living and the dead.
43789: Christ's self-giving and the apostles' lives are a fragrance to God; Malachi foresees incense offered to God among the nations.
43790: A golden incense altar stood before the veil. Incense offered to other gods, or by the wrong person, brought judgement (2 Chr 26:16-21; Jer 44:17-23).
43791: Frankincense is among the Magi's gifts (Matt 2:11). Revelation pictures heavenly worship with incense, joining prayers to God's action on earth.
43792: Whether incense should be used in Christian worship today is a matter of tradition: Orthodox, Catholic and some Anglican churches use it; most Protestant churches do not, reading Revelation's incense as purely symbolic.
43796: A thick embroidered curtain separated the Most Holy Place, where God's presence dwelt, from the rest of the tabernacle and temple. Only the high priest went behind it, once a year. When Jesus died, the Gospels say the temple curtain tore from top to bottom.
43797: Separation between a holy God and sinful people
43798: Hebrews says the curtain showed that 'the way into the holiest' was not yet open.
43799: Access to God opened through Christ
43800: Hebrews links the curtain to Christ's flesh: through his death believers may draw near with confidence.
43802: Some scholars read the tearing mainly as a sign that God was leaving or judging the temple, anticipating its destruction; others combine both readings.
43804: A different object. Paul uses Moses' veil for a lack of understanding that is removed when one turns to the Lord.
43805: Woven with cherubim, the veil echoed the cherubim guarding Eden. Isaiah promises God will destroy 'the veil that is spread over all nations' (Isa 25:7).
43806: All three Synoptic Gospels record the tearing (Matt 27:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45). Hebrews builds a theology of access on it.
43807: Which curtain tore (the inner veil or the outer one at the entrance) is debated; Hebrews' interpretation fits the inner veil.
43809: The ark was a gold-covered wooden chest kept in the Most Holy Place. It held the stone tablets of the law and was topped by the 'mercy seat' with two cherubim. It was treated as God's throne or footstool on earth, the place where he met his people.
43811: God is 'enthroned between the cherubim'; the ark is his footstool.
43813: It held the tablets of the law; manna and Aaron's staff were kept with it.
43815: Blood was sprinkled on the lid on the Day of Atonement. Paul calls Christ a hilasterion, the Greek word used for the mercy seat; whether he means 'mercy seat', 'propitiation' or 'place of atonement' is discussed.
43817: The ark could not be treated as a lucky charm (1 Sam 4) or handled carelessly.
43819: Catholic and Orthodox tradition sees parallels between Mary carrying Jesus and David bringing the ark (leaping, 'how can the ark/mother of my Lord come to me', three months). Many Protestant scholars see the parallel as possible but unproven.
43820: The ark leads Israel across the Jordan (Josh 3), is captured and returned by the Philistines, brought to Jerusalem by David, and placed in Solomon's temple. It disappears from history, likely when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC; Jeremiah says a time will come when it is no longer missed (Jer 3:16).
43821: Hebrews describes its contents; Revelation sees 'the ark of his covenant' in God's heavenly temple (Rev 11:19).
43822: Noah's ark is a different Hebrew word (tevah) and a different object. Claims that the ark of the covenant survives today (for example in Ethiopia, held by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church at Aksum) are traditions that cannot be checked.
43826: Stones last, so people set them up to remember what God had done. God wrote his law on stone. The Bible also calls the Messiah the cornerstone and calls believers 'living stones' built into God's house.
43828: Jacob's pillar at Bethel, the twelve stones from the Jordan, and Samuel's Ebenezer ('stone of help').
43829: Law written in stone, and hearts of stone
43830: God promises to replace a stony heart with a heart of flesh; Paul contrasts tablets of stone with the Spirit writing on hearts.
43832: The New Testament applies the rejected stone to Jesus, now the key stone of God's building.
43834: The same stone is a foundation for some and a stumbling block for others.
43836: The church is a spiritual house built from people joined to Christ.
43838: A stone 'cut without hands' crushes the statue of empires and becomes a mountain filling the earth.
43839: Altars of uncut stone, memorial heaps, stone tablets, and the stone that destroys the empires in Daniel. Stoning was also a method of execution (Lev 24:14).
43840: The cornerstone texts are among the most quoted Old Testament passages in the New. Jesus says the stones would cry out if his disciples were silent (Luke 19:40); the risen Christ gives a white stone with a new name (Rev 2:17).
43844: In a dry land water means life, but floods and deep seas mean danger and death. The Bible uses water both ways: as cleansing and new life, and as the chaos God conquers.
43845: Chaos and death that God controls
43846: Creation begins with God ordering the waters; the flood undoes creation; drowning is a picture of distress.
43848: Washing with water removed ritual impurity; God promises to sprinkle clean water on his people.
43850: John explains that the 'living water' Jesus promised meant the Spirit.
43852: Israel passed through the sea, Noah through the flood; the New Testament compares this to baptism.
43853: Water from the rock, wells of the patriarchs, the bronze basin for priests, and Ezekiel's river flowing from the temple to heal the Dead Sea.
43854: Jesus is baptised, walks on water, turns water into wine, offers living water, and washes feet. The new creation has the river of the water of life.
43855: What 'born of water and the Spirit' (John 3:5) means is debated: baptism, natural birth, or the cleansing work of the Spirit described in Ezek 36:25-27. See /debates/baptism.
43862: Fire gives light and warmth but also burns and destroys. The Bible uses it for God's holy presence, his judgement, the purifying of his people, and the Holy Spirit.
43864: The burning bush, the pillar of fire and the fire on Sinai; 'our God is a consuming fire'.
43866: Fire from the LORD consumed the offering.
43868: Sodom, Nadab and Abihu, and the final judgement.
43870: Like metal in a furnace, people and their work are tested and refined.
43871: The Holy Spirit and God's word
43872: Tongues like fire at Pentecost; God's word burns in Jeremiah's bones.
43873: God appears in fire; the altar fire was never to go out (Lev 6:13); judgement falls as fire. Daniel's friends survive the furnace with a fourth figure (Dan 3:25).
43874: John promises baptism with the Spirit and fire. Jesus speaks of the fire of Gehenna (Mark 9:43-48). Revelation's lake of fire is the final judgement.
43875: Whether the fire of final judgement is literal, a picture of destruction, or a picture of purifying is a core part of /debates/hell. The texts use fire for all three ideas in different places.
43878: Light lets people see, live and find their way. The Bible's first creative word is 'Let there be light', and light runs through Scripture as a picture of God himself, of truth, of goodness and of salvation.
43880: God is light and in him is no darkness at all.
43882: God's word gives light; people in darkness see a great light.
43883: Jesus as the light of the world
43884: John presents Jesus as the true light coming into the world.
43886: Israel and then the church are called to be a light to the nations.
43888: In the end God himself is the light; no sun is needed.
43889: Creation light, the pillar of fire, the priestly blessing ('make his face shine', Num 6:25), and Isaiah's promises of light dawning on the nations.
43890: John's Gospel makes light versus darkness a central theme. Paul calls believers 'children of light' (Eph 5:8; 1 Thess 5:5). Jesus' face shines like the sun at the transfiguration.
43896: Darkness is where you cannot see and danger hides. In the Bible it can mean chaos, judgement, ignorance, evil and death. Yet God is not afraid of darkness, and sometimes hides himself in it.
43898: God separates light from darkness and names both.
43899: The ninth plague, the day of the LORD as darkness, darkness at the crucifixion, and the 'outer darkness'.
43901: People love darkness because their deeds are evil; God rescues from the domain of darkness.
43902: The hiddenness and mystery of God
43903: Moses approached the thick darkness where God was. God is beyond human sight.
43904: Darkness is not dark to God
43905: No darkness hides anyone from God, and he rules over it.
